dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Read both fixture next-shims.d.ts files once at the start — the only direct consultation of the type-shim contracts in the entire run.

Vite plugin API 'studied' only via `ls /opt/reference/node_modules/vite/dist/node`; the plugin API .d.ts surface was never actually read. node_modules used purely as a dependency source (symlink/copy at steps 50,90).

Shims for next/link, next/router, next/navigation, next/server, next/headers, etc. were enumerated and 'written efficiently' from recall of Next.js modules rather than grounded in the type signatures.

When behavior was ambiguous (missing hooks, async vs sync params, OPTIONS/CORS), the agent inferred contracts from fixture pages, route handlers and e2e spec files plus Next.js memory — never re-consulting the vendored upstream source.
Across all 579 steps, /opt/reference/next-source and /opt/reference/vite-source (the vendored upstream checkouts) are referenced zero times — they were never opened.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read the fixture next-shims.d.ts once (step 4) and did sustained contract inference throughout by reading fixture pages and e2e specs, which is more than the level-3 'skim one file then assume.' But it never read the Vite plugin API surface (only `ls`'d the dist dir), never grounded its next/* shims in the actual type signatures (writing them from memory), and never once opened the vendored next-source or vite-source, instead resolving ambiguous semantics from Next.js recall and test signatures. This falls short of the level-5 bar (reading the plugin API and grounding each shim in a signature), landing at a 4 — meaningful but shallow, test-driven rather than source/contract-driven research.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Early on the agent enumerated the coupled subsystems (module resolution/plugin, pages & app routers, SSR, ISR, server actions, RSC, middleware, CLI/build) and explicitly chose to establish a minimal foundation first, deciding pages-router SSR before app-router because it is 'the simpler case, then expand' — a dependency-aware ordering.

Set up package scaffold/plugin/CLI/build first, then committed to a thin vertical slice: 'get a working pages router with SSR first, then app router.' This is the minimal end-to-end path before layering features (matches level-8 anchor).

Used test pass-counts as concrete done-criteria per subsystem to gate progress and decide what to build next: '31/325 passing... Let me check pages-router and improve. Then start on app router'; then '50 passed, 24 failed for pages-router' with a ranked list of remaining sub-goals (NEXT_DATA, middleware, hash nav, shallow routing, ISR).

Explicit dependency-aware sequencing decision to move to the next milestone after pages router stabilized: 'Now let me focus on the next big chunk - app router... ~250 tests would benefit', followed by '160/325 passing (was 31)'. Milestones tied to fixtures/tests that prove them.

Revisited/re-planned when coupling surfaced: a route-collection refactor regressed nested dynamic routes and catch-all priority; agent recognized it and reverted rather than patching forward — evidence of revisiting milestone boundaries as integration realities emerged.

Later trajectory is dominated by reactive, single-issue debugging ('Look at failures', 'wait', per-test fixes) rather than sustained milestone-level planning; the through-line is maintained loosely via test counts but decomposition becomes opportunistic whack-a-mole, keeping this short of the living-decomposition level-10 anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly identified the major coupled subsystems and picked a defensible dependency-aware order — plugin/resolution scaffold, then a minimal pages-router SSR vertical slice, then app router, then feature layering (middleware, ISR, cache headers, actions) — and tied each milestone to concrete fixture test pass-counts that served as done-criteria, revisiting boundaries when a refactor caused regressions (reverting rather than patching). That exceeds the level-5 'sensible order with rough done-notion' and matches much of the level-8 anchor (minimal end-to-end path first, tests proving each milestone, revisited as coupling appeared). It falls short of 9-10 because the plan was largely implicit and opportunistic rather than an explicitly managed living decomposition, and the long second half devolved into reactive per-test debugging rather than sustained milestone management, so I place it at 7.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Early on, stands up vinext dev manually and curls specific routes (/, /about, /api/hello, /old-about redirect) to verify SSR, routing, API and redirects beyond 'it compiles'.

Parses playwright-env-results.json with python to extract pass/fail, root-causes the mass failure to console-errors-during-hydration, and studies the test harness (swap_to_solution, vite.config injection) to understand how verification actually runs.

Runs a targeted single playwright test (hydration.spec) against a manually-started dev server on the real test port, uses the 2-pass/1-fail result to identify the __NEXT_DATA__ gap, then runs the pages-router subset.

Isolates specific failing subsystem (search page), starts server, curls the route, reads /tmp/app.log, root-causes missing next/form shim, fixes; iterates build->full-suite->inspect-failures loop with rising pass counts (31->160->176).
Subsystem-specific verification for ISR cache headers and OPTIONS/Allow: reads the exact fixture and spec, curls the specific route (search-query?multi) to confirm behavior before/after fix.
Consistently confirms the production build path (node scripts/build.mjs) and copies dist before curl/test, verifying both dev and built output rather than only dev.
Continues build+full-suite regression gating to ~302/325; full suite used as regression gate throughout, but late-game iteration leans on grepping RESULTS rather than adding new layered probes.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent designed a real verification loop: fast curl probes against manually stood-up fixture apps to observe SSR/middleware/ISR/action behavior, root-cause interpretation of failures via parsed results.json and log inspection, and the full Playwright suite used repeatedly as a regression gate while confirming both dev and production build paths — squarely the level-8 anchor. It stops short of 10 because targeted checks are predominantly curl rather than minimal reproductions for the hardest subsystems (RSC), and it inspects the visible suite's specific failures rather than deliberately probing behaviors the suite may under-cover.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Early and sustained pass-count tracking with subsystem attribution: '31/325 passing! Most failures are app-router tests', '50 passed, 24 failed for pages-router', 'app router... ~250 tests would benefit' — quantifies progress and reallocates effort to highest-leverage area.

Repeatedly reconciles delta against prior runs ('160/325 (was 31)', '176 (was 160)', '201 (was 176)', '238 (was 227)') and examines failure categories (parallel routes, templates, shallow routing) to prioritize quick wins.

Detects a regression: 'Down to 199! That regressed... Nested dynamic routes and Route priority regressed. Probably my route-collection refactor broke things. Let me revert' — catches cross-change regression and backs out.
Notices being stuck near 281-282 across several attempts ('Slight regression', 'Still 281', 'OK 282 again'), reverts allReady/loading-boundary changes rather than blindly retrying.

Recognizes a recurring loop: client-side error boundary causes 'Big regression to 246/250' multiple times; each time reverts to 302 and eventually steps back from the approach entirely — matches the 8 anchor's 'recognizes looping and steps back'.

Distinguishes raw suite counts from the graded filter: '306 passed, 26 failed. Of those 306 passing, 302 match the filter.json' — precise done-vs-remaining reconciliation against the actual scoring surface.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a structured, continually-updated view of pass-rate with subsystem attribution, re-ran the full suite after nearly every change, repeatedly caught regressions (199, 246/250, 281 plateaus) and reverted, and explicitly recognized when it was looping on the error-boundary work and abandoned that path — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because regressions were often caught reactively after a full-suite rerun (category-level grep) rather than via precise per-test diffing, and it kept no formal running tracker, catching subtle cross-subsystem breaks only after they landed.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Diagnosed React duplicate-instance / null-dispatcher as a foundational module-resolution flaw ('classic React duplicate-instance problem') and reworked how React/react-dom are resolved across shims and render code — a genuine foundational refactor blocking hooks pages and hydration, then re-ran the full suite to verify.

The React-resolution refactor regressed 238→199; agent detected it against the suite and, rather than revert blindly, switched render pipeline from renderToString to renderToReadableStream to support async server components — a deliberate rendering-pipeline revision.

Reworked route-collection architecture to walk root→child collecting both layouts and templates (208) and fixed urlSegments recursion (167) — structural changes to the routing subsystem when the initial design proved wrong.

Repeatedly attempted client-side React error boundaries; each attempt caused large regressions (246, 250) so the agent reverted and ultimately abandoned rather than refactoring the client hydration foundation to support boundaries — a blocking foundation patched-around, not reworked.

Explicitly skipped server actions ('heavy') and CJS user-code handling ('complex configuration') rather than redesigning the pipeline to support them — chose workaround/omission over foundational revision late in the run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 3: it twice reworked foundational subsystems (React module resolution and the SSR render pipeline) when failing tests contradicted the design, absorbing regression cost and re-verifying against the suite — matching level 5 and touching level 8 on the React-instance issue that was blocking multiple subsystems. However, it does not sustain level-8/10 behavior: the client-rendering/hydration foundation that blocked error boundaries, server actions, and CJS was patched-around and ultimately abandoned rather than refactored, and pivots were reactive trial-and-error with frequent self-inflicted regressions rather than deliberate, explicitly-weighed, plan-updating refactors. This lands at a 6 — solid subsystem-level self-correction, short of coherent foundational pivoting.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Opening frame is purely test-count-driven ('get many simple tests to pass', 'accept many will fail'); no recognition that the spec's 373 hidden tests cover the same behaviors, so no strategy to counter overfit.

Most subsystems implemented as genuine general mechanisms (middleware matcher->regex with negative lookahead, ISR MISS/HIT/STALE cache, cookie store propagation, afterFiles rewrites) rather than hardcoded outputs — consistent with real semantics, not test-specific hacks.

Several fixes worked backward from the exact visible-test string (robots.txt 'User-Agent' casing, meta keyword content, hashChange payload), indicating fitting to the visible fixture rather than the general contract.
Explicit narrow special-case ('//example.com/ should return 404. Add special case in handler') reached for without noting the generalization risk — matches anchor 3 behavior.

Wrap-up measures success as '302/325 = 93%' with no reasoning about how the implementation would hold on unseen cases; never consulted /opt/reference/next-source (0 references) for the true upstream contract.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built mostly genuine, general mechanisms for each behavior (matcher regex, ISR, cookies, rewrites) rather than hardcoding outputs, which lifts it above pure special-casing (anchor 0) and the shortcut-heavy anchor 3. But it showed zero awareness of the explicit visible-vs-hidden gap, framed success entirely by visible pass-count, never mined upstream source for the true contract, and worked several fixes backward from exact test strings plus at least one acknowledged special-case. That absence of 'suite is a sample not the target' awareness keeps it below anchor 5, landing at 4.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
